lessons.title: Why you need an AI policy
lessons.subtitle: Shadow AI, Article 4 and what a policy does

sections.title: Shadow AI in practice
sections.content:
> **At work:** For people who implement or govern AI use in an organization. You add jurisdiction, sector, worker representation, contracts and existing security rules to the template yourself.

The sales lead uses a meeting bot, the working student a browser extension, the assistant the new writing feature in the office suite, and nobody asked. That is shadow AI (block 2): AI use outside the approved inventory and the intended controls. Free chat services and locally installed models can create the same unknown data flows and unclear accountability.

A policy sets which purposes are allowed and which systems are approved, which data, recipients and decisions are involved, and who reviews new cases and handles incidents. It works only once tied to inventory, technical controls, training, procurement, data protection, information security and an approval process staff know and use.

sections.title: The obligation: Article 4 since February 2025
sections.content:
Article 4 of the EU AI Act has applied since 2 February 2025. Since the amendment by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, providers and deployers must take measures supporting the development of AI literacy in their staff and other people dealing with the operation and use of AI systems on their behalf. Technical knowledge, experience, education and training, use context and the people or groups affected must be taken into account.

The Article requires no guaranteed level of competence for every individual, no standard attestation and no fixed training format. Providers and deployers need traceable building blocks such as roles, permitted tools, data rules, review routines, escalation and documented training.

The AI policy is one of these blocks and not complete evidence under Article 4. Depending on the use case, training, inventory, risk classification, data protection review and further internal processes may be added.

quiz.questionText: Since when has Article 4 of the EU AI Act applied?

answerOptions.text: Since 1 January 2024
Since 2 February 2025
From August 2026
It is not in force yet

quiz.explanation: Since 2 February 2025. In its current form, providers and deployers must take measures supporting the development of AI literacy in people acting on their behalf.

quiz.questionText: Which description of shadow AI is most accurate?

answerOptions.text: Only AI systems that run at night
Every local AI installation, approved ones included
AI services or functions used outside the approved inventory and intended controls
Only free chat services without user accounts

quiz.explanation: Price, provider and hosting location do not decide it. Shadow AI is use whose purpose, data flow or accountability sits outside the approved controls; an approved local installation is not shadow AI.

sections.title: Parts 1 to 3: scope, approvals, data
sections.content:
The template has six sections and is not a compliance framework that fits every case. Depending on the use, procurement, copyright, product safety, high-risk duties, transparency, worker representation or export control may be added.

**1. Scope and definitions:** Which people, entities, systems, functions and use types does the document cover?

**2. Inventory and approvals:** Which product version, feature, configuration and integration is approved for which purpose, and who decides?

**3. Data and decision rules:** Which data classes, rights, recipients and impacts are permitted? Which uses are prohibited or require case-specific review?

sections.title: Parts 4 to 6: review, incidents, ownership
sections.content:
**4. Review and human responsibility:** Builds on the three-step review from block 4. Which controls apply at each impact level? Who may approve the result, and when is dual control or specialist legal, security or domain review required?

**5. Incidents and escalation:** Which internal reporting channel applies, and which information and evidence must be preserved? Who assesses a data breach, security incident, faulty decision or provider event?

**6. Ownership, changes and review:** Who maintains the policy and inventory, and which events trigger immediate review? How are versions, approvals and communication documented?

Organization and risk decide the length. A short policy can be enough when inventory, approval matrix and operating procedures are maintained separately and linked without ambiguity.

quiz.questionText: How many baseline sections does this course template use?

answerOptions.text: 3 parts
4 parts
6 parts
10 parts

quiz.explanation: Six, as a scaffold you adapt.

quiz.questionText: Which part of the AI policy rests directly on the three-step review from block 4?

answerOptions.text: Part 2: Inventory and approvals
Part 3: Data and decision rules
Part 4: Review and human responsibility
Part 6: Ownership and review

quiz.explanation: Part 4 takes over the three baseline questions from block 4 and sets review depth, approvers and additional controls by purpose and impact.

lessons.title: Exercise: complete the policy
lessons.subtitle: Fill in the template for your organization

sections.title: The template: scope, tools and data
sections.content:
Enter the responsible units and people in the template. While a bracketed placeholder remains, the policy is not ready for approval.

**1. Scope:** [Organization] specifies which workers, contractors, sites, systems, functions and work devices the policy covers. Link the definitions to the current AI inventory.

**2. Approval matrix:** For each entry, record product, version or tier, feature, integration, purpose, data classes, responsible person, contract, region, retention, permissions and approval date. Any combination of purpose, feature and data class not listed stays blocked until it is reviewed.

**3. Data and decision rules:** Refer to your organization's classification and set rules for data minimization, rights in content, permitted recipients, secrets and credentials that are never entered, decisions affecting people and a contact point for questions.

sections.title: Review requirement, escalation and signatures
sections.content:
**4. Review and approval:** Set controls by impact, such as source checks, calculation verification, specialist approval, dual control or a prohibition on automated decisions. Name the person who answers for the final result.

**5. Incident reporting:** Workers report a processing error without delay through [reporting channel] and preserve the time, system, account, input data, output and actions already taken, without deleting or altering evidence on their own. [Incident Response], information security, data protection and other responsible functions assess the case under the existing procedure.

Where a personal data breach has occurred, the controller decides, based on the risk, whether GDPR Article 33 requires notification to the supervisory authority. If so, it is made without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours after becoming aware. Internal deadlines are set in the incident-response plan.

**6. Ownership and review:** Name [Policy Owner], the regular review date and the triggers for immediate review, such as new features, changed contracts, incidents and legal changes. Record the version, approvers, effective date and communication; who has to approve follows the organization's governance.

quiz.questionText: Why does the policy prohibit free AI tools such as ChatGPT Free?

answerOptions.text: Because they deliver worse results than paid versions
Because unapproved consumer offers usually lack a reviewed DPA and binding data controls
Because they are available in English only
Because they need an internet connection

quiz.explanation: Such services usually lack a reviewed DPA, binding data controls and an agreed data region; whether inputs flow into training depends on product and settings.

quiz.questionText: Which statement describes GDPR Article 33 correctly?

answerOptions.text: Every processing error must be reported externally within 24 hours
Only the employee involved decides whether notification is required
The controller assesses the risk; if notification is required, it is made without undue delay and where feasible within 72 hours after awareness
Notification is allowed only once the technical investigation is complete

quiz.explanation: Article 33 ties the duty to a personal data breach and the controller's risk assessment. The 72 hours run from the controller's awareness; no 24-hour duty exists for every processing error.

sections.title: Your five working documents
sections.content:
1. **AI inventory** with functions, purposes, data and owners.
2. **Example data classification** your organization still has to adapt.
3. **Four task patterns** for email, meetings, data analysis and reports.
4. **Output review** as a starting point for risk-based controls.
5. **AI usage policy** linking everything else.

A document is finished only when the placeholders are replaced, the assumptions checked, the owners named and the approvals documented.

sections.title: Next steps
sections.content:
The policy can be one documented building block of AI literacy measures under Article 4. Before it takes effect:

1. **Review and approve:** Bring in the functions responsible for governance, data protection, information security, procurement and worker representation.
2. **Connect operations:** Link the inventory, approval matrix, technical controls, procurement and incident response with unambiguous references.
3. **Teach by role:** Every affected person must be able to apply permitted purposes, boundaries, review duties and the reporting channel in daily work.
4. **Control review:** Document a risk-based regular date and immediate review triggers.

Daily use shows whether the policy works: staff find the right approval, systems are technically bounded, and incidents actually get reported and handled.

quiz.questionText: How many documents come out of the whole course?

answerOptions.text: 2 documents
3 documents
5 documents
8 documents

quiz.questionText: What is the most important next step once the AI policy exists?

answerOptions.text: File the policy and dig it out when needed
Get it approved, connect it to operations, teach it by role, set review triggers
Wait until the EU issues further requirements
Hire an external consultant to implement it

quiz.explanation: In a folder it does nothing. It works when responsible functions approve it, controls implement it, people can apply it and defined events trigger a review.
